intro: Experiments find that small acts of giving and kindness raise the giver's mood a little, and field data show that most bystanders do step in when someone is hurt. The effects are modest and vary by method, so treat these as low-cost habits, not cures.

items.title: Prosocial Spending and Well-Being: Cross-Cultural Evidence for a Psychological Universal
items.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (author copy, McGill University)
items.finding: Survey data from 136 countries linked prosocial spending to greater happiness, and experiments in Canada, Uganda, India and South Africa found that spending on others raised positive feeling.

items.title: Prosocial spending encourages happiness: A replication of the only experiment reported in Dunn, Aknin, and Norton (2008)
items.finding: A larger replication (N = 133) did not find a significant difference using the original analysis, though a more direct happiness measure did point in the original direction.

items.title: The Emotional Rewards of Prosocial Spending Are Robust and Replicable in Large Samples
items.publisher: Current Directions in Psychological Science, Association for Psychological Science
items.finding: A review of all 15 preregistered prosocial spending experiments called the evidence somewhat mixed but argued the emotional benefits hold up in large samples, especially when people choose how to give.

items.title: Happy to help? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of performing acts of kindness on the well-being of the actor
items.publisher: Journal of Experimental Social Psychology (Bournemouth University repository)
items.finding: Across 27 experiments (N = 4,045), performing kind acts raised the doer's well-being by a small-to-medium amount (delta = 0.28), with no sign of publication bias.

items.title: The Association Between Prosocial Behavior and Mental Health: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
items.finding: Pooling 366 effect sizes (N = 222,866), prosocial behavior and better mental health were positively correlated (r = 0.26), with the link differing by culture, measure and study design.

items.title: Would I be helped? Cross-national CCTV footage shows that intervention is the norm in public conflicts
items.publisher: Neuroscience News, reprinting a Lancaster University release on the American Psychologist study
items.finding: Footage of 219 public conflicts in three countries showed that at least one bystander, and typically several, helped in about nine of ten cases.

items.title: I Am Aware of My Inconsistencies but Can Tolerate Them: The Effect of High Quality Listening on Speakers' Attitude Ambivalence
items.publisher: Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin (author page, University of Haifa)
items.finding: Across four laboratory experiments, being listened to by an empathic, non-judgmental listener changed speakers' attitude structure, in line with the idea that good listening lowers defensiveness.

limits: Most kindness studies are short, use self-reports, and show small effects that shrink in some replications; the bystander footage covers street conflicts in three countries, not every setting. These sheets do not claim that any single act changes your life, and nothing here is health advice.
